details:
**Driest non-polar desert on Earth**
The Atacama, in northern Chile, is the driest hot (non-polar) desert in the world. Some weather stations there have never recorded rain, and parts of it go years at a time with no rainfall. This is the most common giveaway.

**Rain shadow of the Andes and the Coastal Range**
The Atacama is so dry partly because it sits between two mountain barriers: the Andes, including the Cordillera Domeyko, to the east and the Chilean Coastal Range along the Pacific. These block moisture from reaching the desert, creating a rain shadow.

**Humboldt Current**
A cold ocean current that flows north along the west coast of South America. It cools the air above the ocean, and together with a stationary high-pressure system over the Pacific it creates a temperature inversion that stops rain clouds from forming.

**Camanchaca (fog) and fog catchers**
Camanchaca is the thick coastal fog that rolls in from the Pacific over the desert. Hills called lomas get most of their moisture from this fog (called garúa in Peru), and towns such as Chungungo have used large mesh "fog catchers" to collect drinking water from it.

**Saltpeter (sodium nitrate) and nitrate ghost towns**
The Atacama holds the world's largest natural deposits of sodium nitrate (saltpeter), which was mined heavily in the 19th and early 20th centuries for fertilizer and explosives. When synthetic nitrates replaced it, the mining towns were abandoned, leaving behind around 200 ghost towns.

**War of the Pacific (1879–1883)**
A war fought largely over the nitrate-rich Atacama, in which Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia. Chile took the coastal provinces, including Antofagasta and Tarapacá, which left Bolivia landlocked.

**Very Large Telescope (Paranal Observatory)**
A telescope run by the European Southern Observatory on Cerro Paranal, made up of four main 8.2-meter units named Antu, Kueyen, Melipal and Yepun, words from the indigenous Mapuche language. The desert's dry, clear skies make it one of the best places on Earth for astronomy, and ESO also runs the La Silla Observatory in the region.

**Extremely Large Telescope (Cerro Armazones)**
A giant telescope being built by the European Southern Observatory on Cerro Armazones, near Paranal. When finished it will be the largest optical telescope in the world.

**Antofagasta and Iquique**
Major port cities on the Atacama coast. Antofagasta is the capital of the Antofagasta Region, and Iquique is the capital of the Tarapacá Region, which contains many abandoned saltpeter mines; both grew because of nitrate and copper mining.

**Mars-like soil (perchlorates)**
Atacama soil is so dry and has such high levels of perchlorates (salts also found on Mars) that scientists use it as a model for Martian soil and to test equipment and methods for detecting life on Mars.

**Lithium and the Salar de Atacama**
The Salar de Atacama is a huge salt flat whose brines hold some of the world's largest lithium reserves. Lithium mining there has been blamed for disturbing the flamingos that live in places such as Chaxa Lagoon.

**Chuquicamata copper mine**
One of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world, owned by Codelco, Chile's state copper company. Copper mining is central to the economy of the Atacama and of Chile as a whole.

**Tamarugal Plain and the Loa River**
The Pampa del Tamarugal is a large inland basin in the northern Atacama, named for the drought-tolerant tamarugo tree. The Loa River, Chile's longest river, flows through the desert to the Pacific.
